newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-IAAF DEFENDS DECISION TO SUSPEND SLANEY.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-IAAF DEFENDS DECISION TO SUSPEND SLANEY.

text.p: International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) president Primo Nebiolo defended the decision to suspend American runner Mary Slaney after a positive dope test.
The IAAF, which announced its decision Saturday, was annoyed that Slaney's case had dragged on for nearly a year in the United States with no sign of a resolution.

"The IAAF has rules and when a federation does not follow the rules we have to do something," Nebiolo said in an interview with Reuters Sunday. "We were not happy we were obliged to take this decision but it had to be taken."
The 38-year-old Slaney, twice world champion, was found to have unusually high levels of testosterone in her body at the U.S. Olympic trials in June last year.

She was allowed to continue competing, pending hearings into her case, and finished seventh in her preliminary race in the 5,000 metres at the Atlanta Olympics and second in the 1,500 metres at the world indoor championships in Paris in March.

Until the IAAF announcement that she would be suspended until U.S. officials decided on her case, Slaney had said that she intended to compete in the USA Track and Field championships this month, with the aim of qualifying in the 1,500 metres for the world championships in Athens in August.
Slaney's husband Richard accused the IAAF of "acting with malice" and said Saturday that they were exceeding their powers.
But Nebiolo said sports federations had to take doping seriously and act swiftly to stamp it out.

"We have to be serious and I hope that national federations and other sports bodies will be serious in the same manner. If we are serious the battle against doping will be successful, if not we will lose," he said.
"We will continue this campaign (of suspensions) because this is our duty. In a family the most grave care that the parents could have is some of their children taking drugs.
"Personally, I love all my athletes and I am very sad when one of them makes a mistake," Nebiolo said.
Nebiolo said the IAAF council were almost united in their decision to suspend Slaney and fellow American runner Sandra Farmer-Patrick, another American runner who tested positive for testosterone.
"The case of the Americans was not provoked by Nebiolo. It was a decision of 27 persons. If not unanimous, it was taken with a great majority," he said.
In Indianapolis USATF spokesman Pete Cava called Nebiolo's remarks "ridiculous."

"We have been through this before and didn't expect to see the same thing happen again," Cava said, referring to the celebrated Butch Reynolds' case in which the U.S. Supreme Court upheld Reynolds' right to run in the 1992 U.S. Olympic trials after he had been banned by the IAAF for an alleged positive doping test.
"We are surprised and disappointed by the IAAF's actions," Cava said of the IAAF council's suspension Saturday of Slaney and Farmer-Patrick.

Cava would not comment directly when asked whether Slaney, who has not been suspended by the U.S. federation pending the outcome of a U.S. hearing procedure, would be permitted to run in the U.S. championships June 11-15 in Indianapolis.
"That would be violating the confidentiality of the case," he said. "But there have been precedents," he said, citing the Reynolds case.

Then the IAAF overruled a USATF decision to allow Reynolds to compete domestically, but Reynolds' attorneys obtained a court injunction permitting him to do so and the case went to the U.S. Supreme Court, where a justice ruled in Reynolds' favour.

But Reynolds, the 400-meter world record-holder, was never allowed to run internationally until his four-year ban expired and the U.S. courts eventually ruled in the IAAF's favour in a $27 million suit by Reynolds seeking damages in the case.
